text: Every QAOA circuit and every quantum annealer you'll encounter is built to minimize an Ising Hamiltonian, not a QUBO directly. The good news: QUBO and Ising are the same problem wearing two different costumes, and the translation between them is one clean substitution.

The Ising model comes from statistical physics: a lattice of spins, each plus-1 or minus-1, with total energy H of s equal to the sum of local-field terms h_i times s_i, plus coupling terms J_ij times s_i times s_j. The bridge to QUBO's 0-1 binary variables is the substitution s_i equals 1 minus 2 x_i. Check it: x_i equals 0 gives s_i equals plus 1, spin-up; x_i equals 1 gives s_i equals negative 1, spin-down. This is exactly why Ising, not QUBO, is the native language of quantum annealing hardware.

Converting Lesson 2's QUBO, f of x1, x2 equals negative 5 x1 minus 3 x2 plus 2 x1 x2, by substituting x_i equals 1 minus s_i over 2 and expanding algebraically term by term produces the Ising Hamiltonian: H equals negative 3.5 plus 2 s1 plus 1 s2 plus 0.5 s1 s2. Checked against all four binary assignments directly, every single one matches the original QUBO exactly -- including the minimum of negative 6, still achieved at the same underlying choice, selecting both.

Here's why this matters for hardware. A qubit's Pauli-Z operator has eigenvalues of exactly plus 1 and minus 1 -- the same two values an Ising spin takes. That is not a coincidence; it's the entire reason QUBO problems can be loaded onto quantum hardware at all. The translation pipeline for every problem in this course runs the same way: real-world problem, to QUBO, to Ising Hamiltonian, to quantum circuit or annealer schedule. Nothing about the optimum changes along the way -- only the coordinate system describing it does.

Next lesson runs that full pipeline end-to-end on Max-Cut, the 'hello world' of quantum optimization -- deriving its QUBO from scratch and converting it into the cost Hamiltonian that QAOA's circuit is actually built around.
